analysis.one_liner: Requires hospitals and health insurers to meet federal cybersecurity standards, with audits, fines, and Medicare help.
analysis.headline: The Senate bill to tighten health-sector cybersecurity died in the Senate Finance Committee without a hearing or a vote, after being introduced in September 2024 with one cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would set minimum and enhanced cybersecurity requirements for hospitals, insurers, and any company that handles health data, and require each one to run annual risk analyses and stress tests, publish its compliance status online, pay for an independent security audit, and pay a fee to fund government oversight. Companies that failed to report or comply could face fines of up to $5,000 a day, and executives who filed false compliance statements could face felony charges. To ease the burden, Medicare would pay hospitals up to a combined $1.3 billion to adopt cybersecurity practices, while hospitals that refused would eventually see Medicare payments reduced by up to 1%, and providers whose claims processing was knocked out by a cyberattack could get advance Medicare payments. The bill never got a committee hearing or vote before the two-year congressional session ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients and everyone whose medical records are held by a hospital, insurer, or health data company. Stronger security standards, mandatory stress tests, public disclosure of compliance, and real penalties would lower the odds that a ransomware attack cuts off prescription fills, surgery schedules, or claims payments — the kind of disruption that leaves sick people stranded and billing systems frozen for weeks.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients and anyone with health records

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Health and Human Services Secretary to adopt minimum security requirements for all covered health entities and tougher requirements for companies whose failure would cripple access to care, updated at least every two years [S2]

Requires each covered entity and business associate to conduct annual security risk analyses, document disaster-recovery plans, run real-world stress tests of whether they could keep patient care running after a cyber incident, and publish their compliance status on a public website [S2]

Requires an annual independent security audit of every covered entity, plus annual Secretary-led audits of at least 20 companies, with priority for systemically important firms and repeat offenders [S2]

Requires each covered entity and business associate to conduct annual security risk analyses, document disaster-recovery plans, run real-world stress tests of whether they could keep patient care running after a cyber incident, and publish their compliance status on a public website [S2]

Requires CEOs and chief information security officers to personally sign annual compliance statements, with felony penalties of up to $1 million and 10 years in prison for knowingly filing false reports [S2]

Sends $800 million in fiscal 2027-2028 and $500 million in 2029-2030 from the Medicare hospital trust fund to help hospitals — prioritizing rural, Puerto Rico, Indian Health Service, and other high-needs hospitals — adopt essential and enhanced cybersecurity practices [S2]

Lets doctors' offices, nursing homes, hospices, and other Medicare providers hit by a cyberattack that disrupts claims processing receive accelerated or advance Medicare payments so a breach at a billing company doesn't bankrupt them [S2]

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals, insurers, and health data companies would bear compliance costs: annual risk analyses, stress tests, independent audits, a user fee for oversight (capped at $40 million in 2026, $50 million in 2027, growing with inflation), and higher penalties for violations — at least $500 for unknowing violations up to at least $250,000 for willful neglect. Hospitals that don't adopt the required practices face Medicare payment reductions reaching 1% by 2033. Some of these costs would likely be passed on to patients and premiums.
analysis.who_pays_short: Hospitals, insurers, and health data companies

drawbacks.text: Compliance is expensive, especially for small and rural hospitals already on thin margins; the bill responds with Medicare incentive payments and hardship waivers, but the eventual payment reductions (up to 1% of Medicare rates by 2033) could still squeeze struggling facilities [S2]
The user fee on covered entities would be passed through hospital budgets and insurance premiums, so patients would partly finance the oversight of the companies holding their data [S2]

The bill strips administrative and judicial review of the Secretary's decisions about which companies face enhanced requirements and how Medicare payments are adjusted, meaning companies could not challenge those determinations in court [S2]

A good-faith objection: prescriptive federal security mandates can lag real threats and impose paperwork costs that outpace security gains for smaller providers; the bill's two-year update cycle and waiver authority partially answer this [S2]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real: patients get a health system far less likely to be paralyzed by a cyberattack, and companies that hold sensitive medical records get clearer rules and upfront Medicare money to comply. The costs — compliance paperwork, audits, fees, and possible payment cuts — fall on the health industry and partly on patients through prices. The strongest design concerns are the removal of judicial review of key agency decisions and the burden on small rural providers, which the bill tries to soften with targeted payments and waivers rather than fully solving.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in late September 2024 and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it sat without a hearing, markup, or vote until the congressional session ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Ron Wyden introduced the bill in the Senate on September 25, 2024, joined by Sen. Mark Warner [S1]
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance the same day [S4]
The only other recorded action was the referral; no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever took place [S4]
The bill had a single cosponsor, Sen. Mark Warner, a Democrat [S3]
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill died with it [S1]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospitals, insurers, and health data companies are better off because the bill died — they avoid new security mandates, annual audits, user fees, executive accountability, and higher penalties. Patients and communities vulnerable to health-sector cyberattacks got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Hospitals, insurers, and health data companies

industries.note: Hospitals would face mandatory security standards, annual audits, stress tests, and user fees, plus Medicare payment cuts up to 1% for noncompliance — but also $1.3 billion in Medicare incentive payments tilted toward rural and high-needs hospitals. Their interest in avoiding compliance costs runs against patients' interest in care that survives a cyberattack.

industries.industry: Health insurers and health data clearinghouses
industries.note: As covered entities and business associates, they would owe annual risk analyses, independent audits, public compliance disclosures, oversight fees, and much higher penalties, including personal executive accountability. The bill's safeguards protect the patients whose data and claims they handle.
The bill creates a mandated annual independent-audit requirement for every covered health entity, a large new compliance market. Their service is the public good being purchased.
